content: Steroid diabetes is a medical condition characterized by prolonged hyperglycemia that arises as a result of glucocorticoid therapy administered for another underlying medical condition. This condition is often transient but not always. The most common glucocorticoids responsible for inducing steroid diabetes are prednisone and dexamethasone, which are typically given systemically in pharmacologic doses over a period of days or weeks. Steroid diabetes frequently develops during high-dose glucocorticoid treatment for conditions such as severe asthma, organ transplantation, cystic fibrosis, inflammatory bowel disease, or induction chemotherapy for leukemia or other cancers. Glucocorticoids counteract the action of insulin and stimulate gluconeogenesis, particularly in the liver, leading to an overall increase in hepatic glucose production. While most individuals can produce sufficient additional insulin to compensate for this effect and maintain normal glucose levels, those who cannot develop steroid diabetes. The diagnostic criteria for steroid diabetes are the same as those for diabetes mellitus. These include fasting glucose levels persistently above 125 mg/dL (7 mmol/L) or random glucose levels exceeding 200 mg/dL (11 mmol/L) in the context of high-dose glucocorticoid therapy. Insulin levels in affected individuals are usually detectable and may even be elevated, but they are insufficient to adequately control blood glucose levels. In severe cases, hyperglycemia may become extreme enough to result in nonketotic hyperosmolar coma. Management of steroid diabetes depends on the severity of hyperglycemia and the anticipated duration of glucocorticoid therapy. Mild hyperglycemia in an immunocompetent patient may not require treatment if the glucocorticoids are expected to be discontinued within a week or two. However, moderate hyperglycemia increases the risk of infections, particularly fungal infections, especially in individuals with other risk factors such as immunosuppression or the presence of central intravenous lines. Insulin is the most commonly used treatment for managing steroid-induced hyperglycemia. It is important to differentiate steroid diabetes from other causes of hyperglycemia, such as stress hyperglycemia, hyperglycemia due to excessive intravenous glucose administration, or new-onset diabetes of another type. Glucocorticoid therapy can also precipitate type 1 or type 2 diabetes in individuals who are already in the process of developing these conditions. Consequently, it is not always possible to determine whether apparent steroid diabetes will resolve after glucocorticoid therapy is discontinued or whether it will persist as a permanent condition. More commonly, undiagnosed cases of type 2 diabetes are unmasked during glucocorticoid treatment, as subclinical hyperglycemia worsens and becomes symptomatic. In general, steroid diabetes that occurs in the absence of preexisting type 2 diabetes resolves upon cessation of glucocorticoid therapy. It is also worth noting that steroid diabetes does not occur with other types of steroid hormones, such as anabolic steroids, mineralocorticoids, or sex steroids, as these categories of steroids have minimal impact on glucose metabolism.
